definition.text: Apache Kafka is a distributed event store and stream-processing platform that keeps messages in a durable log so many consumers can read them.

facts.text: Kafka is an open-source distributed event store and stream-processing platform, written in Java and Scala.
The project aims to provide a unified, high-throughput, low-latency platform for handling real-time data feeds.
Kafka is a distributed log-based messaging system that guarantees ordering within individual partitions rather than across the entire topic.
Unlike queue-based systems, Kafka retains messages in a durable, append-only log until they expire, so multiple consumers can read at different offsets and pull at their own pace.
Kafka can handle multiple producers and consumers while providing disk-based data retention and high scalability.
Kafka Connect moves data in and out of external systems, and the Kafka Streams libraries support stream-processing applications.
Kafka was originally built for massive log processing and is used for log analysis, data streaming such as recommendations, system monitoring and alerting, and change data capture.
Kafka Raft (KRaft) uses the Raft algorithm for metadata management.

definition.text: Kafka organizes messages into topics split into partitions, written by producers, read by consumer groups and stored on a cluster of brokers.

facts.text: The message is the basic unit of data in Kafka, like a record in a table consisting of headers, a key and a value.
Every message goes to a topic, which is like a folder on a computer, and topics have multiple partitions.
Producers create new messages, batch them, send them to a topic, and balance messages across the partitions.
Consumers work together as a consumer group to read messages from the broker.
A Kafka cluster consists of several brokers, and each partition is replicated across multiple brokers to ensure high availability and redundancy.
The partition-based design enables fault isolation and parallel processing: a consumer that delays committing an offset stalls only its own partition while other partitions remain unaffected.

In 2025 Kafka added share groups as an alternative to consumer groups, giving queue-like semantics with individual acknowledgment and allowing more consumers than partitions, where consumer groups assign each partition exclusively.

definition.text: Kafka can lose messages at the producer, the broker or the consumer unless acknowledgments, replicas and offset commits are configured carefully.

facts.text: Many developers believe Kafka by design guarantees no message loss, but its architecture and configuration decide how and when it might lose messages.
producer.send() does not send directly to the broker: the application thread puts the message in a record accumulator, and a separate sender (I/O) thread sends it.
The producer needs proper acks and retries settings to make sure messages reach the broker.
A healthy broker cluster should not lose messages, but messages are usually flushed to disk asynchronously for higher I/O throughput, so an instance that goes down before the flush loses them.
Replicas must be properly configured to hold a valid copy of the data, because determinism in data synchronization is important.
Auto-committing might acknowledge records before they are processed, so if the consumer goes down mid-processing, some records may never be processed.
A good practice is to combine asynchronous commits in the processing loop for higher throughput with synchronous commits in exception handling so the last offset is always committed.
Kafka uses manual offset management, giving consumers control over retries and failure handling.

definition.text: Kafka is fast mainly because it relies on sequential disk I/O and the zero-copy principle for sending data to consumers.

facts.text: Two design decisions carry the most weight in Kafka's performance: its reliance on sequential I/O and its focus on efficiency through the zero-copy principle.
Kafka's message-set abstraction groups messages, which leads to larger network packets and larger sequential disk operations and turns a bursty stream of random message writes into linear writes.
Without zero copy, data is loaded from disk to the OS cache, copied to the Kafka application, copied to the socket buffer, then copied to the network card.
With zero copy, the OS cache copies the data directly to the network card via the sendfile() command, saving multiple copies between the application and kernel contexts.

definition.text: Kafka Streams is a Java library for building stateful, scalable and fault-tolerant stream-processing applications on top of Kafka.

facts.text: Kafka Streams is a stream-processing library written in Java for stateful stream-processing applications that are scalable, elastic and fully fault-tolerant.

Its main API is a domain-specific language with high-level operators such as filter, map, grouping, windowing, aggregation, joins and tables; the lower-level Processor API implements custom operators and can be mixed with it.
For stateful processing it keeps local operator state in RocksDB, which can write to disk so the state can be larger than main memory.
For fault tolerance all updates to local state stores are also written to a topic in the Kafka cluster, so state can be recreated by reading those topics back into RocksDB.

definition.text: Change data capture identifies and captures the changes made to data in a database so they can be replicated and synced to other systems.

facts.text: CDC is a set of design patterns for determining and tracking data that changed, an approach to data integration based on identifying, capturing and delivering changes made to enterprise data sources.
Constant data changes leave databases, data lakes and data warehouses out of sync, and CDC replicates and syncs data across multiple systems to overcome this.
In CDC the source is the system with data believed to have changed, and the target is the system that needs to act on the changed data.
A CDC tool monitors the database transaction logs through a source connector to capture inserts, updates and deletes.

Captured changes are transformed, published to a message queue and propagated to targets such as data warehouses, analytics platforms and distributed caches like Redis, where a sink connector consumes the log and updates the targets in real time.
A popular CDC solution uses Debezium with Kafka Connect to stream changes from source to target with Kafka as the broker, and Debezium has connectors for MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and more.
In the push model the source creates a snapshot of changes and delivers rows downstream; in the pull model the downstream target requests the data from the source.

definition.text: CDC can detect changes with timestamp, version-number or status columns, with triggers that log events to a queue table, or by reading the database transaction log.

facts.text: With a timestamp column, any row stamped more recently than the last capture is considered changed.
With version numbers, changed rows are marked with a version; at capture all data with the latest version is considered changed, and the reference table then gets a new version number.
A status column can mark a row as changed, or can complement the other methods by showing that a row with a new version or later date should not yet be updated on the target.
Using time, version and status together is a particularly powerful mechanism, because the three elements are not redundant.
With triggers, events on the transactional table are logged into a queue table that can later be played back to replicate the data to a target.
Transaction-log based CDC has minimal impact on the database, needs no application changes, and can replay the original transactions in the order they were committed.
Reading transaction logs is hard because no standard exists for their format, most databases do not document it, and uncommitted changes later rolled back must be eliminated.

definition.text: Stream processing is a programming paradigm that treats streams, or sequences of events in time, as the central input and output objects of computation.

facts.text: Stream processing, also called event stream processing or distributed stream processing, views streams, or sequences of events in time, as the central input and output objects of computation.
It encompasses dataflow programming, reactive programming and distributed data processing.
Data is treated as an unbounded, continuous sequence of elements rather than a static dataset.
Given a stream, a series of operations called kernel functions is applied to each element, and uniform streaming, where one kernel function is applied to all elements, is typical.
The program defines a dataflow sequence and the execution environment applies the kernel automatically as new elements arrive; kernels can also do aggregation windows or stateful modifications.

The paradigm simplifies parallelism by restricting the kinds of parallel computation allowed, and it exploits data parallelism: the same function applied to all records lets many records be processed simultaneously.

It sacrifices some flexibility for easier, faster and more efficient execution, working well for data-centric workloads but less well for general-purpose processing with random data access, such as databases.
Batch processing collects data and processes it all at once, as in daily billing, while stream processing handles data in real time, as in fraud detection.

title: Stream processing engines
article: Stream processing#Distributed and cloud-scale execution ecosystems

definition.text: Distributed stream processing engines are grouped by execution model into native continuous engines, micro-batch engines and distributed logging fabrics.

facts.text: Native continuous engines process elements individually as they arrive, optimizing for sub-second, real-time latencies.

Apache Storm is a native low-latency real-time computation system; Apache Flink treats batch computing as a specialized subset of continuous streaming; Apache Samza is a stateful engine built over Apache Kafka.
Micro-batch engines collect incoming elements into small time windows to achieve high-throughput stream semantics; Apache Spark Streaming processes live data in small discrete chunks.
Distributed logging fabrics, such as Apache Kafka, serve as the persistent, append-only transport layer, and managed services such as AWS Kinesis and Google Cloud Dataflow run streams in the cloud.

definition.text: Complex event processing runs continuous queries over event streams to detect patterns and infer higher-level events from simpler ones.

facts.text: A continuous SQL query is an ongoing query that processes incoming data based on timestamps and window duration.
Joining a stream of stock orders with a stream of trades can output every order matched by a trade within one second of the order being placed.
A complex or composite event is the high-level event inferred from constituent events; for example, bells ringing, a man in a tuxedo, a woman in a gown and rice thrown can together signal a wedding.
